titleText.en: The TempurPedic wineglass guy broke his ankle.
titleText.noteEn: The official title text adds a deadpan mishap for the mattress demonstrator associated with an upright wineglass.

regions.labelEs: HACERSE ARRUMACOS CARA A CARA ESTÁ BIEN, PERO NUNCA SABEMOS QUÉ HACER CON LOS BRAZOS INFERIORES.

applications.explanationEn: Hacerse and arrumacos form the mutual-affection expression, and the attached se indicates that the affectionate action is exchanged.
The two copies of cara and the fixed link a form the reusable face-to-face expression.

regions.labelEs: SUS BRAZOS INFERIORES ENTRAN EN EL OPORTUNO HUECO.
TÍO, ESO SIEMPRE ME HA MOLESTADO.

applications.explanationEn: Ha supplies the present-time helper, and molestado is the completed-action form that stays unchanged after it.

regions.labelEs: AUNQUE... ¿ENTONCES LOS BRAZOS SIMPLEMENTE SE QUEDAN COLGANDO?

applications.explanationEn: Se and quedan form the matching version of quedarse, while colgando names the continuing hanging state.

cards.answerEn: to give each other; helps express mutual affection with arrumacos
cards.noteEn: Hacer normally means ‘to do’ or ‘to make.’ Its attached se can show that two or more people exchange the action. In hacerse arrumacos, the whole expression describes affectionate cuddling or caressing.

example.en: The friends give each other gifts.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that people cuddle or exchange affectionate caresses with each other?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by arrumacos.
cards.noteEn: Hacerse arrumacos is a conventional expression for mutual affectionate touching. In the dictionary form, se is attached to hacer. With a stated subject, the matching short word usually stands before the changed verb: nos hacemos arrumacos or se hacen arrumacos.

example.es: La pareja se hace arrumacos en el sofá.
example.en: The couple cuddles on the sofa.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that people are directly facing one another or meeting in person?
cards.answerEn: Use cara a cara after the action or state.
cards.noteEn: Cara a cara works as one expression meaning ‘face-to-face.’ The fixed a stays between the repeated word cara. It can describe physical orientation or a direct personal conversation or meeting.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links the two copies of cara in cara a cara
cards.noteEn: In cara a cara, a is a fixed middle link. Translate the three words together as ‘face-to-face’ rather than giving a its usual direction meaning.

cards.answerEn: our here; Spanish uses los before a body part whose owner is already clear
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before a body part when the surrounding verb or context already identifies its owner. Natural English often supplies ‘my,’ ‘your,’ ‘our,’ or another possessive word instead.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
Sus is used before plural things that are owned. It agrees with what is owned, not with the owner; with usted, it can mean formal “your.”
Entrar often means ‘to enter’ or ‘to go in.’ With an object and an opening or available space, it can say that the object fits into that space.

example.es: Las cajas entran en el armario.
example.en: The boxes fit in the cupboard.

cards.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Molestado is the completed-action form of molestar, ‘to bother’ or ‘to annoy.’ After ha, it stays unchanged even when the affected person changes.
Uno can stand in for a masculine singular noun that has already been mentioned or is obvious from the situation, just as English can use ‘one.’

example.en: I need a pencil; give me one.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks quedarse, “to remain” or “stay”
cards.noteEn: Quedar and quedarse have several uses. With se here, the subject continues to be present rather than leaving.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone remains in, or ends up in, a particular state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of quedarse followed by a word that names the resulting or continuing state.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign in the prompt means that the state word follows quedarse. Quedarse is pronominal: it comes with me, te, se, nos, or os even though no one literally remains themselves. Change quedar and its small marker to match the person and time. When another verb has already changed for the person, the marker may stand before that verb: se puede quedar.

example.es: Después de la noticia, Pablo se quedó callado.
example.en: After the news, Pablo fell silent.

cards.noteEn: With se, quedan is a present-time form of quedarse. It says that several people or things continue in, or end up in, the state named next.
Colgando is the ongoing-action form of colgar, ‘to hang.’ For an action verb ending in -ar, this form normally replaces -ar with -ando; it can describe something that remains suspended or dangling.

cards.answerEn: you all do; you all make (informal plural, mainly Spain)
cards.noteEn: Hacéis is the present-time form of hacer used with vosotros, the informal ‘you all’ used mainly in Spain. In most of Latin America, speakers normally use ustedes hacen instead.

cards.answerEn: them (masculine or mixed group, after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: Ellos usually means ‘they,’ but after a preposition such as con, para, or sin, English uses ‘them.’
Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.
Hicimos is the completed-past ‘we’ form of hacer, ‘to do’ or ‘to make.’ Hacer changes its stem to hic- in this past tense, and hicimos has no written accent.
Grande shortens to gran directly before a singular noun. Here it describes importance or significance rather than physical size.
